analysis.one_liner: Applies federal antitrust laws to railroads, ending their special exemption from merger and competition rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House committees until Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Railroads have long been exempt from the antitrust laws that apply to nearly every other industry. This bill would have removed that exemption, meaning railroad mergers, rate agreements, and coordinated pricing could be challenged in court like any other industry's. It was sent to two House committees, then to a railroads subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that ship goods by rail — farmers, manufacturers, utilities, and other freight customers — would gain the ability to challenge railroad mergers and coordinated rate-setting under the same antitrust rules everyone else lives under. That competition pressure could ultimately lower shipping costs passed on to consumers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clayton Act so that the antitrust exemption for common carriers no longer covers railroads, restoring the application of the antitrust laws to rail carriers.
It strikes related exemptions in Title 49 and the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973, so railroad agreements and mergers would no longer be carved out from antitrust review.
The CRS summary describes the bill as eliminating the antitrust exemption applicable to railroads.

analysis.who_pays: Major freight railroads would bear the cost: they could no longer merge freely or set joint rates with immunity from antitrust suits, and they would face potential litigation over existing and future agreements.

drawbacks.text: Railroads argue the Surface Transportation Board already reviews mergers and rate disputes, so adding antitrust suits would duplicate regulation and create legal uncertainty about which rules apply.

Because rail is a capital-intensive industry with high fixed costs, critics of applying antitrust law worry that litigation over joint agreements could complicate the cooperative arrangements railroads use to interchange freight across the national network.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Removing the exemption would put railroads under the same competition rules as other industries, a clear gain for captive shippers who currently have little leverage over rates. The main cost is the risk of duplicated or conflicting regulation, since a federal board already oversees railroad mergers and rates. The tradeoff favors shippers and consumers, but the bill was narrow and never advanced, so it was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Transportation committees, then to the Railroads subcommittee, and never came up for a hearing or vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Green of Wisconsin, joined by Rep. Earl Pomeroy, introduced the bill on July 18, 2005.
It was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure for the provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill had 9 cosponsors, 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans, but never reached a committee vote or the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major freight railroads benefited from the outcome: their exemption from antitrust law remained intact, with no new competition review of mergers or rate agreements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Freight railroads, who kept their antitrust exemption

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from the start, with 5 Democratic and 4 Republican cosponsors, and no vote or recorded opposition ever showed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the railroads' exemption from antitrust laws, exposing their mergers and joint rate agreements to competition review and possible lawsuits. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against shippers and consumers who pay rail rates.

industries.industry: Rail shippers (farm, manufacturing, and energy freight customers)
industries.note: Shippers with little choice among rail carriers would gain a new legal tool to challenge mergers and coordinated pricing that raise their shipping costs, savings that could pass through to consumer prices.
